The study was conducted on single-crystal Rene N5 turbine blades using 45-150 μm Rene N5 powder.
The LENS system used a 1000W Nd:YAG laser focused to a 0.5mm spot size.
In the initial feasibility specimen 190-0, a crack extended from the top surface to the middle of the third deposited layer.
EBSD analysis of specimen 190-0 showed the deposit had the same crystallographic orientation as the substrate.
The parametric variation study examined the effects of surface finish (as-EDM, ground, polished) and deposition parameters (laser power, velocity, layer thickness).
X-ray radiographs of the parametric variation specimens confirmed that cracking occurred during deposition, not sample preparation.
Cracking was observed to be directionally dependent, occurring primarily in the [100] direction of the single-crystal substrate.
Attempts to control the thermal gradient (G) to solidification velocity (v) ratio by preheating the substrate and introducing dwell times did not prevent cracking.
Deposition trials on the actual turbine blade surface showed epitaxial deposition was possible on arbitrarily oriented single-crystal surfaces.
The columnar grain growth orientation in the blade surface deposits matched both the <100> substrate direction and the local thermal gradient.
The study found that the epitaxial deposition mechanism was related to both the substrate orientation and the thermal conditions during solidification.
Cracking was a persistent issue throughout the study, suggesting stability and reproducibility problems with the LENS system used.
The main difficulties encountered were the development of cracks in the deposits and the unreliability of the LENS system.
The study examined the effects of surface preparation, surface geometry, and crystallographic orientation on the deposited microstructure.
Grain multiplication, where dendrite arms are re-melted and separated, was observed as a mechanism contributing to crack formation.
